drafts.topic: Loss aversion: why "don't miss out" beats "get this"

post.hook: Why does “don’t miss out” sell better than “get this”?
slides: People feel **loss aversion**: losing feels worse than gaining feels good.
Our ancestors prioritized **survival instinct** to avoid threats.
A limited-time offer feels like a **missed deal**, triggering loss pain.
Use **scarcity language** like “only 2 left” or “ends soon” to spark urgency.
A/B test: **loss-framed** copy lifts clicks 10-15% over gain copy.
post.takeaway: Swap “get this” for “don’t miss out” and watch conversions climb.
post.caption:
Ever notice how a countdown timer makes you click faster than a simple “Buy now” button? It’s not magic, it’s psychology.

When we think we might lose an opportunity, our brain lights up the same fear circuits that kept our ancestors safe from real danger. That fear is called **loss aversion**, and it’s stronger than the pleasure of gaining something identical.

Marketers exploit this by using **scarcity language**, phrases like “only 2 left” or “ends tonight”. In tests, the loss-framed copy often outperforms gain-framed copy by 10-15% in click-through rates.

What loss-focused wording will you try in your next campaign?

drafts.topic: Starbucks: why the smallest cup on the menu is called Tall

post.hook: Why does Starbucks call its smallest cup “Tall”?
slides: Starbucks introduced **Tall** in 1996 to replace **short** and sound more positive.
The **framing effect** shows positive wording shifts perception of value.
Calling a cup “Tall” frames it as generous, even if volume matches a “short”.
Customers feel they’re getting more, so they’re willing to pay the same price.
Small businesses can rename modest options with upward-slanted terms to boost perceived size.
post.takeaway: Rename “basic” plans as “Premium Lite” to increase sign-ups without changing features.
post.caption:
Ever wondered why the smallest Starbucks cup isn’t called “Short”? The brand swapped it for “Tall” to sound more appealing.

Psychology tells us that positive framing changes how we evaluate size and value. When a cup is labeled “Tall,” it feels larger, even if the actual volume is unchanged.

That tiny shift can make customers comfortable paying the same price, thinking they’re getting more. You can apply the same trick to your offerings.

What other product names could you re-frame for better perception?

fact_check.claim: Starbucks introduced the Tall size in 1996 to replace the short size.
Framing effect influences perception of value with positive wording.
Customers perceive “Tall” as larger and are willing to pay the same price.
fact_check.source: General consumer research on framing, various studies
